content: @Adam Topaz and I are trying to understand if mathlib has any ways to talk about group (co)homology without mentioning any actual homological complexes, @Joël Riou maybe you know something about this?

module

public import Mathlib.Algebra.Homology.DerivedCategory.Ext.EnoughProjectives
public import Mathlib.RepresentationTheory.Rep.Iso

universe u

open CategoryTheory

variable {k G : Type u} [CommRing k] [Group G]

instance : HasExt.{u} (Rep.{u} k G) := hasExt_of_enoughProjectives _

def Rep.GroupCohomology (A : Rep.{u} k G) (n : ℕ) : Type u :=
  Abelian.Ext (Rep.trivial k G k) A n
It seems we don't have HasTor, so we can't do something similar for group homology...

In #32840, I am trying to remove the old Ext API, so that we should at least get an isomorphism with this definition of group cohomology (which does not refer to a specific complex, even though there is the whole machinery of derived categories under the hood).

I guess if we want to stay as general as possible, we could even use CategoryTheory.Functor.IsLeftDerivedFunctor and CategoryTheory.Functor.IsRightDerivedFunctor and state things in terms of arbitrary functors which satisfy the property of being left/right derived functors of (co)invariants.

I have a formalisation of Tor via the derived monoidal category structure #homology > Derived hom and tensor @ 💬 but it will take a certain time before it reaches mathlib. (My priority is to have everything related to functors in one variable first.)
Here, we could use the left derived functor of coinvariants.

I am starting with right derived functors first:

  • #43063 feat(CategoryTheory): right Kan extensions and Guitart exact squares

• #39128 feat(CategoryTheory): triangulated derived functors using derivability structures

(and some more to come)

@Jack McCarthy -- The question is writing down statements about group cohomology, say, without referring to any particular implementation. One way to do it is to write down a statement of the form: "Let F be the functor M \mapsto M^G. For all functors H, if H satisfies IsRightDerivedFunctor F, then blah blah blah." We know that all such H will be isomorphic to H∗(G,M)H^*(G,M)H∗(G,M) in some canonical way, so in practice you just need to prove this assertion for a single H, but this way you can choose your own implementation

Adam Topaz said:

We know that all such H will be isomorphic to H∗(G,M)H^*(G,M)H∗(G,M) in some canonical way

Nit: actually one has to give a huge amount of data to make this isomorphism canonical, something which is essentially never done in practice, giving rise to sign issues in this so-called "canonical" identification.

Example: we all imagine that we know the formula for the boundary map H^0(G,C)->H^1(G,A) associated to a short exact sequence of G-modules, and it's of the form "given a G-invariant element c of C, lift randomly to b in B, and observe that gb and b both map to c so their difference maps to 0 and is thus in A, and that's the 1-cocycle", but is the difference gb-b or b-gb? Both work fine and as far as I can see, neither is "right" or "wrong" but if someone chooses one and someone else chooses the other then their H^1's are identical but need to be identified via the -1 map.
CategoryTheory.Functor.rightDerivedNatIso CategoryTheory.Functor.rightDerivedUnique
Yeah, by "canonical" here I mean "as right derived functors"

I'm trying to reconcile our two points of view and I'm having trouble understanding the generality in which mathlib's theory of right derived functors is set up. The predicate docs#CategoryTheory.Functor.IsRightDerivedFunctor claims that if C,D,H are categories, if L:C->D makes D a localization of C, if F:C->H and RF:D->H are functors, and if we have some extra data consisting of a natural transformation alpha: F -> (RF o L), then we can ask if RF is a right derived functor of F. I am unclear about what these things are in practice for, say, group cohomology. Is the idea that C is some kind of chain complexes of G-modules, D is the derived category, H is Ab, and I'm not quite sure about F (is it H^0(ker(d)/im(d) at 0) or something)?

The example I like to carry around is the following universal delta functor: take the usual universal delta functor for group cohomology (which is more than a set's worth of data as it is a choice of boundary map for every n and every short exact sequence) and then change all delta:H^37(C)->H^38(A) by a minus sign. We get a new universal delta functor with identical cohomology groups but non-identical extra data. But the induced "canonical" isomorphism of group cohomology with itself which is +1 on H^n(G,M) for n<=37 and -1 for n>=38. Is this extra data buried in alpha in the mathlib set-up?

Kevin Buzzard said:

Is the idea that C is some kind of chain complexes of G-modules, D is the derived category

Yeah, it's essentially like this (except I think H would be something like D(Ab)? I haven't looked too closely). You get an induced functor on the level of complexes (maybe modulo homotopy), then take the (total) derived functor which gives you a functor in the derived category. I think in this case it would indeed be better if we had some abstraction of the sort IsUniversalDeltaFunctor or something like this, but we don't, and I guess one reason is that the derived category approach is considered a more "modern" approach to such things.
You can look at the implementation of docs#CategoryTheory.Functor.rightDerivedFunctorPlus to see how you get right derived functors in the "usual" sense from the mathlib sense.
I asked codex to spell out the relationship with what we currently have in mathlib, and this is what it came up with.

Kevin Buzzard said:

identical cohomology groups but non-identical extra data. But the induced "canonical" isomorphism of group cohomology with itself which is +1 on H^n(G,M) for n<=37 and -1 for n>=38. Is this extra data buried in alpha in the mathlib set-up?

This isomorphism would not commute with the connecting homomorphism given by exact sequences 0 -> M' -> M -> M'' -> 0 (so this is not an iso of delta-functors [unless we also change them as you pointed out!]). There will be surely be some signs shenanigans whichever route is taken!

Adam Topaz said:

Yeah, it's essentially like this (except I think H would be something like D(Ab)? I haven't looked too closely). You get an induced functor on the level of complexes (maybe modulo homotopy), then take the (total) derived functor which gives you a functor in the derived category. I think in this case it would indeed be better if we had some abstraction of the sort IsUniversalDeltaFunctor or something like this, but we don't, and I guess one reason is that the derived category approach is considered a more "modern" approach to such things.

If F is the invariants functor from Rep k G to ModuleCat k, we have its extension to (bounded below) cochain complexes (or the homotopy category of such complexes) and then we have F.rightDerivedFunctorPlus which is a functor between the corresponding derived categories (along with a natural transformation F.rightDerivedFunctorPlusUnit that is used in order to express the universal property it satisfies). Mathlib does not yet know that this functor is a triangulated functor. "Triangulated" functor is a notion which involves data (the isomorphisms which give the commutation with shifts, Functor.CommShift) and the property that a distinguished triangle is mapped to a distinguished triangle. Once F.rightDerivedFunctorPlus is endowed with this Functor.CommShift instance (see #39117, #39126 and #39128), we can prove that the natural transformation F.rightDerivedFunctorPlusUnit is also compatible with shifts (this is a NatTrans.CommShift instance). [Note here that we could tamper with the signs of the isomorphisms that are part of the Functor.CommShift instance, but this would break the property that rightDerivedFunctorPlusUnit satisfies NatTrans.CommShift.]
Once the API is set up, I would probably recommend using this Functor.rightDerivedFunctorPlus API rather than rephrasing all the additional data and properties it satisfies.
I am not completely convinced that we would need the delta-functor abstraction, because in most situations, we should be able to lift everything at the level of derived categories!

This isomorphism would not commute with the connecting homomorphism given by exact sequences 0 -> M' -> M -> M'' -> 0 (so this is not an iso of delta-functors [unless we also change them as you pointed out!]). There will be surely be some signs shenanigans whichever route is taken!

I am talking about two delta functors from G-modules to Ab, one is "usual group cohomology and usual connecting homomorphisms" and the other is "usual group cohomology and usual connecting homomorphisms except change the sign of all delta_37:H^37(C)->H^38(A)". Both of these satisfy the axiom of a universal delta functor, and so by nonsense we should get isomorphisms between the cohomology groups which commute with all diagrams, and those isomorphisms are "identity on H^n for n<=37 and -identity on H^n for n>=38".

I am not entirely sure what you are saying, but I suspect we are saying the same thing. What I am trying to point out is that if I only have a bunch of functors H^n and another bunch of functors H'^n and they satisfy all the right things (i.e. they both give the right answer), then it is not true that there are canonical isomorphisms H^n=H'^n, we need a lot more data before we get these isomorphisms, this data is typically never mentioned by mathematicians, and furthermore it is not "canonical" in any sense, it amounts to a choice of signs in some sense.
Yes, we agree that we need to be aware of the additional data that are used in order to "rigidify" the canonicity of isomorphisms.

To be more precise about the signs conventions, when taking account the global picture, I have three "concerns":

  1. docs#CategoryTheory.Abelian.Ext.comp is the composition on Ext, given α : Ext X Y a and β : Ext Y Z b, we define α.comp β .. : Ext X Z (a + b) (or more precisely Ext X Z c whenever a + b = c). At some point, I formalised a very draft comparison with the composition of Yoneda Exts which does not involve signs anywhere (but I have no longer maintained this proof for some time as it became more painful to bump mathlib), and there may have been a (−1)ab(-1)^{ab}(−1)ab sign in order to relate the two definitons. In any case, it can be argued that Ext.comp is correct anyway because the mathlib convention for composition is syntactically α.comp β .. rather than βα, so that if we switch the order of two terms of degrees a and b on the paper/screen, we should multiply by (−1)ab(-1)^{ab}(−1)ab!

1. Given a short exact sequence S : ShortComplex C (with hS : S.ShortExact), we have a class in hS.extClass in Ext1Ext^1Ext1 and we use it to define connecting morphisms in the covariant and contravariant long exact sequence of Ext-groups. In #43224, I am starting to investigate how this interacts with the constructor docs#CategoryTheory.InjectiveResolution.extMk I introduced for Ext-groups using an injective resolution of the target (and later I would do the same for projective resolutions of the source), I am not yet sure of the sign in the statement https://github.com/joelriou/mathlib4/blob/ext-mk-comp-extclass/Mathlib/CategoryTheory/Abelian/Injective/Ext.lean#L261-L268 (and I would have even more doubts about the signs in the case of projective resolutions!)

1. In the general derived category set up and in particular docs#CochainComplex.HomComplex I am following closely the signs conventions defined by Brian Conrad in Grothendieck duality and base change, and about the interactions with group cohomology, we may have some sign issues because the HomComplex has the right signs conventions, but when we apply it to a projective resolution P of the trivial representation, then in the HomComplex from (the extension to a cochain complex indexed by ℤ) of P to a representation M (as a cochain complex sitting in degree 0), there are signs, while there are no signs in the currently used "naive" definition docs#ChainComplex.linearYonedaObj (this issue is mentionned by Conrad on page 13 in his book).

In any case, when it becomes relevant, I will try to double-check definitions in mathlib regarding the signs convention of Conrad (which, as far as I understand, are the best according to Gabber, who is the person I know that cares the most about such matters). A consequence is that when computing connecting homomorphisms in terms of explicit cocycles in group cohomology, we may have different signs as compared to part of the existing literature (in which case, we would have to record that in the documentation...).

Let me explain a little bit this explicit cocycle stuff, assume 0 ⟶ M₁ ⟶ M₂ ⟶ M₃ ⟶ 0 is a short exact sequence of representations of a group G, and m₃ : M₃ be invariant under G. Lift m₃ as m₂ by surjectivity. Then, there is a unique 1-cocycle G → M₁ such that after using the inclusion into M₂, we get the map which sends g to g • m₂ - m₂. Should the boundary in H1(G,M1)H^1(G, M₁)H1(G,M1​) be given by this g • m₂ - m₂ or by m₂ - g • m₂? (The future will tell us!)

I have investigated a little bit more about 2. above, and while there was nothing wrong with the definitions/lemmas in mathlib, my current understanding is that it seems that the connecting homomorphism for the contravariant long exact sequence of Ext in Conrad's book is only up to a sign given by the composition of Ext (i.e. the composition of morphisms in the derived category). As a result, I am introducing a new definition Ext.δ in #43492, and in #43224, I show that Ext.δ can be computed "snake lemma style" using an injective resolution of the target https://github.com/joelriou/mathlib4/blob/0cbb295838e45b27515796a1d46224dbe7a696b9/Mathlib/CategoryTheory/Abelian/Injective/Ext.lean#L326
